fatal_errors: Atomic size mismatch cannot be systematically varied while retaining an identical elemental composition; changing the selected elements also changes surface energies, mixing enthalpies, melting points, and chemical affinities, so the proposed comparison cannot isolate size mismatch.

The hypothesis replaces the target surface-energy-driven Au/Cu segregation, diffusion, evaporation, and shape evolution mechanism with unsupported strain-induced local ordering and bulk phase segregation.
The cited evidence does not establish that atomic size mismatch causes high-temperature ordering or segregation in high-entropy nanoparticles.
explanation: The response addresses the broad question of high-temperature stability in equimolar nanoalloys and provides a nominally testable hypothesis and falsification rule, but it does not reconstruct the relevant AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticle system, vacuum heating protocol, temperature range, or observations. Its proposed annealing near or above 1000 °C differs substantially from heating to 973 K and may introduce melting or volatilization mechanisms that are not controlled. The hidden result concerns non-sluggish atomic diffusion driven by surface-energy differences, preferential Au/Cu surface enrichment, shape-dependent mobility, melting or evaporation, loss of small particles, and a 22% size reduction. None of these central outcomes is predicted. The baseline is also confounded because low- and high-mismatch alloys require different chemistries. E1 concerns entropy-stabilized oxides, E2 concerns force-field construction, and E3 concerns compositional fluctuations affecting dislocations; none directly supports the claimed size-mismatch-to-ordering-to-segregation causal chain. Thus, although the alternative is conceivable in some alloy systems, it is neither well isolated experimentally nor supported by the supplied evidence.
